categories.label: Regulatory Mandates and Legislative Mechanisms
categories.memo: Covers hard-law instruments—mandatory scoring systems, assembly rate benchmarks, and legislative reform—used by governments to compel or enable MMC adoption, contrasted with voluntary/market approaches.

codes.label: Mandatory Buildability/Constructability Scoring Systems
codes.description: Government-legislated minimum scores (e.g., B-score, C-score) on land sale sites compel developers to adopt prefabrication techniques, providing enforceable legitimacy beyond voluntary incentives.

codes.label: Mandatory Assembly Rate Benchmarks
codes.description: Government-set minimum prefabrication/assembly rates act as regulatory levers, but if set too high they can discourage adoption by increasing incremental costs and creating market entry barriers for developers.

codes.label: Institutional Legitimacy of Formal Systems vs Voluntary Incentives
codes.description: Formalized, enforceable regulatory systems (codes, mandates) are argued to provide stronger institutional legitimacy and compliance than voluntary or market-based incentive schemes alone.

codes.label: Legislative and Procurement Framework Reform
codes.description: Calls for government legislation to reshape procurement frameworks, local requirements, and social value mandates to remove structural barriers to MMC uptake, including barriers facing smaller firms in public procurement.

codes.label: Insufficient Government Standards and Codes
codes.description: Lack of comprehensive government standards/codes for prefabricated construction (PC) limits effective regulatory supervision of stakeholders and raises costs across design, production and construction phases.

categories.label: Subsidy Design and Optimization
categories.memo: Covers economic modeling and design of government subsidy schemes intended to offset MMC cost premiums, including their limits, interactions with supply chains, and diminishing returns.

codes.label: Cost-Offsetting Subsidy Schemes
codes.description: Direct government funding schemes (e.g., cost premium offset funds, tax reductions) intended to reduce the financial barrier of MMC/DfMA adoption for contractors and developers.

codes.label: Subsidies vs Other Policy Instruments
codes.description: Comparative evidence that financial subsidies are more effective than technical guidelines or compulsory regulations in driving early-stage MC adoption, though effectiveness diminishes as markets mature.

codes.label: Stackelberg/Bilevel Subsidy-Setting Models
codes.description: Modeling of government-contractor interactions as a leader-follower (Stackelberg) game in which government sets subsidy price anticipating contractor responses, addressing uncertainty in costs and volumes ignored by deterministic policies.

codes.label: Diminishing Returns and Subsidy Caps
codes.description: Larger subsidy budgets yield progressively smaller gains in adoption rate, and subsidy caps or ceilings must be carefully calibrated to avoid under-incentivizing adoption while controlling public expenditure.

codes.label: Subsidy Policy Evolution with Cost Maturation
codes.description: As underlying MMC/MC costs fall with technological maturity, required subsidy levels can be reduced while adoption continues to rise, implying dynamic rather than static subsidy policy design.

codes.label: Supply Chain-Wide Subsidy Design
codes.description: Effective subsidy policy must account for the full supply chain (manufacturers, logistics providers) rather than only the government-contractor dyad, including cross-border logistics cost effects on adoption incentives.

categories.label: Contractual Mechanisms for Passing Through Government Incentives
categories.memo: Addresses how government subsidies and policy incentives are operationalized within supply chain contracts between developers, contractors and manufacturers.

codes.label: Revenue-Sharing Contracts for Subsidy Transfer
codes.description: Contracts through which developers pass government subsidies to general contractors to incentivize higher prefabrication/assembly rates, illustrating a specific risk/benefit allocation mechanism.

codes.label: Limits of Simple Incentive Contracts
codes.description: Basic revenue-sharing contracts alone can create profit imbalances (e.g., losses for developers despite contractor gains), showing the need for more sophisticated coordination mechanisms.

codes.label: Transfer Payment Plus Revenue-Sharing Contracts
codes.description: Combined contract structures where contractors bear baseline costs and developers bear incremental subsidy-related investment, enabling fairer risk/cost allocation and win-win outcomes across the supply chain.

codes.label: Centralized vs Decentralized Contractual Decision-Making
codes.description: Cooperative, centralized decision-making between developer and contractor yields higher profit and assembly rates than independent contractual decisions, highlighting efficiency losses in decentralized two-echelon supply chains.

categories.label: Reward-Penalty and Environmental Regulatory Mechanisms
categories.memo: Covers policy mechanisms specifically targeting environmental/emission reduction (ER) performance in prefabricated construction supply chains, and how contractual responsibility is allocated in response.

codes.label: Reward-Penalty Mechanisms vs Subsidies
codes.description: Reward-penalty regulatory mechanisms achieve stronger environmental compliance than subsidy mechanisms but impose greater profit losses on contracting parties, creating a policy trade-off.

codes.label: Contractor as Central Coordinator of ER Commitments
codes.description: The contractor is modeled as the party responsible for committing to overall project-level emission reduction targets, with suppliers responding to that commitment, reflecting real-world contractor-regulator liaison roles.

codes.label: Equal Sharing of Environmental Responsibility
codes.description: Under both reward-penalty and subsidy mechanisms, contractor and supplier tend toward an equal (50/50) split of environmental responsibility, suggesting a natural equilibrium regardless of policy type.

codes.label: Context-Sensitive Policy Selection
codes.description: Policy choice (reward-penalty vs subsidy) should be tailored to regional context—environmentally critical regions favoring reward-penalty mechanisms, economically vulnerable regions favoring subsidies.

codes.label: Inter-Organizational Green Procurement Coordination
codes.description: Recommendations for green procurement contracts or shared emission-reduction targets to align contractor and supplier environmental efforts, extending policy incentives into contractual clauses.

categories.label: Market and Client-Driven Adoption Drivers vs Policy Drivers
categories.memo: Contrasts policy/regulatory drivers with market-based and client/developer decision-making drivers of MMC adoption, including firm-level investment behavior and demand-side barriers.

codes.label: Developer/Client Cognition and Attitude
codes.description: Developer or client misunderstanding of MMC/DfMA benefits, low enthusiasm, and lack of cost-control experience act as demand-side barriers independent of policy incentives.

codes.label: Contractor Capital Investment as Market Driver
codes.description: Firms' willingness to commit upfront capital to establish prefabrication facilities is a market-driven enabler of adoption, distinct from policy-driven mandates or subsidies.

codes.label: Transaction Costs as Hidden Market Barriers
codes.description: Transaction costs from new technology, management processes, and design changes impose hidden cost burdens on developers, reinforcing reluctance to adopt PC absent policy support.

codes.label: Demonstration Projects and Business Models as Soft Policy Tools
codes.description: Government-sponsored demonstration projects and successful PC business models serve as a softer institutional driver to increase developer enthusiasm and acceptance of prefabrication.

categories.label: Contractual Misalignment and Reform for MMC
categories.memo: Addresses how existing standard contract forms are misaligned with MMC processes and the specific clause-level reforms needed, situating these within broader policy/institutional drivers.

codes.label: Misalignment of Traditional Contracts with MMC
codes.description: Standard contracts designed for traditional construction are structurally misaligned with MMC characteristics (offsite manufacturing, different risk profiles), contributing to low adoption.

codes.label: Preference for Standard Forms with Amendments
codes.description: MMC businesses prefer standard forms like JCT for familiarity and workability, but require amendments (e.g., to liquidated damages, retention) to suit MMC delivery, while bespoke forms are often client-imposed for risk transfer.

codes.label: Payment Mechanism Reform for Offsite Financing
codes.description: Traditional progress-payment mechanisms are unsuitable for MMC because offsite manufacturing requires upfront financing not tied to on-site milestones, necessitating contractual reform.

codes.label: Risk and Responsibility Reallocation to Manufacturers
codes.description: Contracts need to reflect the shifted role of manufacturers in design/engineering responsibility and different inspection/sign-off locations under MMC delivery models.
